Listen to this article Share As fears grow that an Ebola outbreak could be used to restrict political campaigns and voter participation, electoral experts are urging INEC and the government to prepare for a public health emergency without compromising democratic rights. The confirmed case of Ebola in Abuja has introduced an unexpected uncertainty into Nigeria’s preparations for the 2027 general elections, raising questions about whether efforts to protect public health could affect political campaigns, voter mobilisation and electoral participation. Although the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has not announced any change to the election timetable, the outbreak has triggered speculation among opposition figures and citizens that restrictions on public gatherings or movement could be introduced as the campaign season approaches. The Federal Government confirmed on October 20 that a woman who recently travelled to Nigeria from Uganda had tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus disease. The patient was receiving treatment in isolation at a private hospital in the Federal Capital Territory, while authorities identified 44 close contacts for monitoring. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention activated its incident management system, with contact tracing and infection-prevention measures intensified to contain the infection. But beyond the immediate public health response, the case has opened a new front in the political debate ahead of elections scheduled for January 16, 2027, for the presidency and National Assembly, and February 6 for governorship and state assembly contests. For opposition parties, the concern is that measures introduced to contain the disease could affect their ability to reach voters, particularly if restrictions are imposed unevenly across political organisations or geographical areas. Read also: Nigeria’s Ebola case related to virus identified in Kenya, says FG Phrank Shaibu, director of strategic communication at the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council, warned against using the outbreak to limit political competition. “The Tinubu administration must not weaponise Ebola to frighten the public, silence its opponents or suppress voter participation. Any public health measure must be backed by clear medical evidence, applied equally and never used as a pretext to interfere with Nigerians’ democratic rights,” Shaibu said in a statement. Similar concerns have circulated on social media, where some users have alleged that the government could use the outbreak to restrict movement after the Christmas holidays and prevent eligible voters from participating in the elections. These claims have not been substantiated by evidence of any government plan to impose such restrictions. The allegations nevertheless illustrate how a public health emergency can become entangled with existing political distrust before an election. For Paul James, an electoral and political process specialist, the priority should be ensuring that the outbreak is managed transparently and that any decisions affecting political activities are guided by public health evidence rather than political considerations. “I think the country and its institutions have demonstrated capacity in the past to manage, to deal with these pandemics,” James said, adding that Nigeria’s previous experience with public health emergencies provided lessons for the current situation. He said transparency in the government’s response and clear communication with the public would be essential as preparations for the elections continued. James argued that any restrictions on political campaigns should be based on assessments by the NCDC and other relevant health authorities, proportionate to the risks identified and limited to affected locations where appropriate. He warned against imposing nationwide restrictions if evidence showed that the outbreak remained localised. “I would discourage a blanket restriction across the country when the evidence does not support that,” he said. The distinction is important because campaign restrictions could have unequal consequences for political parties. Large gatherings, rallies, ward meetings and door-to-door mobilisation remain important tools for candidates seeking to reach voters, while smaller parties may have fewer resources to replace physical engagement with extensive digital campaigns. If public health measures become necessary, the challenge for the authorities will be to protect citizens without creating an uneven playing field for candidates and parties. Lessons from previous outbreaks Nigeria’s experience with Ebola in 2014 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 offers important lessons, although the two emergencies had different effects on public life and electoral administration. During the 2014 Ebola outbreak, Nigeria contained the imported infection through contact tracing, isolation and coordinated public health interventions. The outbreak was declared over in October 2014, months before the February 2015 general elections, limiting its direct overlap with the final election period. The COVID-19 pandemic, however, presented a more extensive challenge. INEC temporarily suspended electoral activities in 2020 as restrictions and public health concerns disrupted normal operations. The commission subsequently published its Policy on Conducting Elections in the Context of the COVID-19 Pandemic, in May 2020. The framework addressed how electoral activities could be conducted while reducing risks associated with physical contact and large gatherings. James said INEC had demonstrated during the pandemic that it could adapt its procedures, including by moving some engagements online and introducing precautions around polling-unit operations. He urged the commission to build on that experience by developing a contingency framework for the 2027 elections before circumstances make emergency decisions unavoidable. The framework, he said, should establish in advance how political parties would conduct campaigns if restrictions became necessary, alongside arrangements for voter education and election-day administration. He also called for closer coordination between INEC, the NCDC, the Ministry of Health, political parties, civil society organisations, security agencies and the media. Such coordination, he argued, would help ensure that public health rules were understood before implementation and that electoral stakeholders had clear channels for raising concerns. “Public health emergencies will continue to test the resilience of democratic institutions,” he said, arguing that protecting lives and safeguarding democracy should not be treated as competing objectives. For Nigeria, the immediate task is to contain the infection. The longer-term test will be whether the institutions responsible for public health and elections can work together to protect citizens while ensuring that an emergency does not become a justification for arbitrary restrictions on democratic participation.
